timeline.label: Early 2nd c. AH
timeline.text: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz encouraged recording

timeline.label: 3rd c. AH
timeline.text: Bukhari (d. 256 AH) and Muslim (d. 261 AH) compiled the sahih collections

timeline.label: Later
timeline.text: Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah: the six books

head: Grade
Meaning
Used for rulings?
rows: Never: not to be quoted as hadith

blocks.h: Grade the chain (invented example chains, not real hadith)

questions.q: Chain 1: every narrator is honest with an accurate memory; each heard it from the one before.
Chain 2: all honest and connected, but Narrator B's memory is good, not excellent.
Chain 3: Narrator C is known for poor memory.
Chain 4: Narrator D is known for lying.
questions.a: Mawdu' (fabricated) or rejected: honesty is a condition; never quote it as hadith.

keywords.def: weak: not relied on for rulings

questions.q: Explain how scholars decided a hadith was sahih.
questions.a: Every narrator honest and precise, the chain connected back to the Prophet ﷺ, and no hidden defect or contradiction.

questions.q: Grade-the-chain task on the pupil PDF: four invented example chains (not real hadith) with narrator notes; decide each grade and give the reason.
questions.a: Grades with reasons based on honesty, memory and connection

questions.q: Extend: why must Muslims not share a mawdu' report as hadith?
questions.a: It is lying about the Prophet ﷺ, which is a grave sin (Bukhari and Muslim).

questions.q: Stretch: why did hadith need recording after the Companions' time?
questions.a: Narrators were dying, the ummah spread far, and some began fabricating.

questions.q: A narrator known for lying makes a hadith ...
questions.a: A) Weak or fabricated. Honesty is a condition; a liar's report is rejected.

questions.q: Think again: how could you check a 1,400-year-old quote?
questions.a: Trace and check the chain of narrators, as hadith scholars did.
